q.intro.text: The parabola y equals x squared minus four x plus thirteen never touches the x axis. Its lowest point is two, nine.

q.ask.text: So how many solutions does x squared minus four x plus thirteen equal zero have, now that you know i? Pick one, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Four steps with the quadratic formula. Press each one: the picture moves first, then the algebra.

e.s0.text: a is one, b is negative four, c is thirteen. b squared minus four a c is sixteen minus fifty two, which is negative thirty six. Negative, so no real number works. That is why the parabola misses the x axis.

e.s1.text: The formula needs the root of negative thirty six. A root of a negative is i times a real root. The root of negative thirty six is i times six, so six i.

e.s2.text: x equals four plus or minus six i, over two. Divide both terms by two: x equals two plus or minus three i. Both roots sit on the line where the real part is two, right above the vertex.

e.s3.text: Check two plus three i. Two plus three i, squared, is four plus twelve i plus nine i squared, which is negative five plus twelve i. Then negative five plus twelve i, minus eight, minus twelve i, plus thirteen, is zero. It works.

e.why.text: Quick check. Why do both solutions have the real part two?

e.w-ok.text: Yes. The plus or minus only touches the root. Negative b over two a, which is two, is in both. The two roots are a conjugate pair.

e.w-opp.text: The opposite of two plus three i is negative two minus three i. The second root is two minus three i: the same real part, and the opposite imaginary part.

e.w-cross.text: The parabola never crosses the x axis. But its vertex is at x equals two. The shared real part is the x of the vertex.

t.intro.text: Your turn: x squared plus six x plus twenty five equals zero. Step one is done. b squared minus four a c is thirty six minus one hundred, which is negative sixty four.

t.root.text: Step two. Write the root of negative sixty four as a number times i.

t.root-ok.text: Yes. The root of negative sixty four is i times eight, so eight i.

t.root-neg.text: Negative eight squared is sixty four, not negative sixty four. The root of negative sixty four is i times eight.

t.root-no.text: The root of negative sixty four is i times the root of sixty four. What is the root of sixty four?

t.split.text: Step three. x equals negative six plus or minus eight i, over two. Type it as x equals a plus or minus b i.

t.split-ok.text: Yes. Negative six over two is negative three, and eight i over two is four i. So x equals negative three plus or minus four i.

t.split-b.text: The formula starts with negative b, and b is six. The top is negative six plus or minus eight i, so the real part is negative three.

t.split-half.text: Divide both terms of the top by two: negative six over two, and eight i over two.

t.split-no.text: Split the fraction. The real part is negative six over two, the imaginary part is eight over two.

t.cb-right.text: At the start you picked two non-real solutions, and you were right. No x intercepts means no real solutions, but the formula still gives a pair.

t.cb-none.text: At the start you picked no solutions. No x intercepts means no real solutions. Over the complex numbers there are two: two plus or minus three i.

t.cb-one.text: At the start you picked one non-real solution. The plus or minus always gives two: two plus three i, and two minus three i.

t.cb-skip.text: A negative discriminant: no real solutions, two non-real ones, a conjugate pair.

p.intro.text: Jordan solved three quadratics. Each time the roots were a conjugate pair, a plus or minus b i. So it is always true, says Jordan. Is that a proof?

p.yes.text: Three examples show three cases. Let’s see what a proof for every real a, b, c looks like.

p.build.text: Right. Examples are not a proof. Build one for every real a, b, c with a negative discriminant. Fill each because.

p.c1.text: Right. Four a c minus b squared is positive, so its root is real, and the i comes out in front.

p.c2.text: Right. A fraction with a sum on top splits into two fractions: the real part, and the imaginary part.

p.c3.text: Right. Both parts are real numbers, so the roots are p plus q i, and p minus q i: mirror images in the real axis.

p.no.ex.text: That is Jordan’s argument. Examples check only the equations you tried.

p.no.opp.text: The opposite flips both parts. The two roots share the real part, negative b over two a.

p.no.conj.text: A conjugate keeps the real part and flips only the imaginary part.

p.no.other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?

p.done.text: That’s a proof. It works for every real a, b, c at once. Non-real roots of a real quadratic always come as a conjugate pair. With non-real coefficients, they need not.
